questions.question: How do you render a list in React, and why does each item need a key?
questions.title: Rendering React lists with keys
questions.direct_answer: Render a React list by transforming data into elements, commonly with `filter` and `map`. Each element created directly in that collection needs a stable key unique among its siblings. React uses the key to match an item with its previous identity when items are inserted, removed, or reordered, preserving the correct DOM and component state.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can connect array transformation with React's identity matching.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding the key inside the extracted row instead of on the element returned by map.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain insertion and reordering rather than saying keys only remove a warning.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Use JavaScript data operations such as `filter` and `map`.
Put the key on the element returned directly from `map`.
A key identifies an item among its siblings.
Use a stable ID from the underlying data.
Keys guide matching; they are not rendered as DOM attributes or passed as normal props.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I render a list by keeping its data in an array and transforming that data into React elements. `filter` chooses which records are visible, and `map` returns one element for each visible record. React can render the resulting array as sibling elements.

The element returned directly from `map` needs a `key` that identifies its data item among siblings. A database ID, persisted UUID, or another stable value from the data is ideal. The key needs to be unique in that one list, not globally unique across the whole application.

React uses keys while reconciling one render with the next. If an item is inserted at the start, stable keys let React match every existing row to the same earlier identity and create only the new row. Without that identity, matching by position can associate a row's local state or DOM with the wrong data.

For example, a contact list can filter contacts by name and map each contact to `<ContactRow key={contact.id} contact={contact} />`. If the list is sorted alphabetically later, each ID moves with its contact, so an expanded row or focused input remains attached to the correct person.

The key belongs where the array is created. If `ContactRow` returns an `li`, placing the key on that inner `li` is too late because the parent is reconciling the `ContactRow` elements. The parent should key each `ContactRow` in the map. Keys are a matching hint for React, not ordinary component input. If the row also needs the ID, I pass a separate `contactId` or the whole contact prop. Good list rendering therefore combines a clear data transformation with stable identity from the data itself.

sections.title: Data becomes siblings with identity
sections.content: Mapping decides what each record looks like. Keys answer a different question: which record in this new sibling collection corresponds to which record from the previous render?

sections.title: Matching matters when positions move
sections.content:
Imagine rows A, B, and C matched only by position. Inserting X first makes the old first position appear to be X even though it previously represented A. Stable keys produce matches A-to-A, B-to-B, and C-to-C, while X is recognized as new.

The visible text may still look correct after a position match because props are updated, but state and uncontrolled DOM values can reveal the mistake. Identity determines which component instance and state belong to each record.

sections.title: Insert one keyed row
sections.content:
Before: [A:a7] [B:b4] [C:c9]
After:  [X:x2] [A:a7] [B:b4] [C:c9]
Matches: a7→A, b4→B, c9→C; x2 is new

sections.title: Filter and map data into keyed rows
Boundary to remember
sections.content: A key only has meaning within its sibling collection. Reusing `id=7` in a separate list is fine. What fails is using the same key twice among siblings or changing one item's key between renders without intending to create a new identity.

questions.question: Why should you avoid array indexes and random values as React keys?
questions.title: Stable keys versus index and random keys
questions.direct_answer: An array index describes a position, not an item's identity, so inserting, deleting, or reordering records can move state to the wrong item. A random key changes on every render, causing React to recreate every row and lose local state or input. Use a stable ID from the data; use an index only for a truly static list.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner understands the correctness consequence of unstable identity.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `Math.random()` to silence the key warning or assuming an index is safe because records currently look correct.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Trace a reordered list whose rows contain local input state.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A stable key follows the same data item across renders.
An index changes meaning when list order changes.
A random key creates a new identity on every render.
Bad keys can move row state or lose user input.
An index is acceptable only when items never reorder, insert, or delete.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A good React key represents the identity of a data item and remains stable while that item exists. An array index represents only the item's current position. Those values are the same only while the collection never changes order.

If a row is inserted, removed, filtered, or sorted, later indexes shift. React may then reuse the component state and DOM at position zero for a different record now occupying position zero. The new props can update the visible label while local state, focus, or an uncontrolled input remains attached to the old position.

For example, imagine editable contacts keyed by index. The user types a draft phone number in the second row, then the list is sorted. The component instance for index one stays at index one even though a different contact moved there, so the draft can appear beside the wrong name.

A random key has the opposite problem: it never matches. `key={Math.random()}` tells React that every row is new on every render. React removes and recreates their subtrees, which loses local state and input, can move focus, and performs unnecessary DOM work.

I use an ID that belongs to the record, such as a database primary key or a UUID assigned when a locally persisted item is created. I do not generate that ID during rendering. If the content itself is unique and stable, a value such as a country code can also be a sensible domain key. An index is acceptable for a fixed presentation whose items will never insert, delete, reorder, or hold identity-sensitive state, such as a static list of three legal notices. Even there, a real data key documents identity more clearly when one exists.

sections.title: Position and identity answer different questions
sections.content: Position says where an item is now. Identity says which item it is across time. Reconciliation needs the second answer whenever a collection can change shape or order.

sections.title: The classic input-state failure
sections.content:
Uncontrolled inputs keep their current value in DOM state. If React reuses that input node for a different data row because an index key stayed in the same position, changing the row label does not automatically replace the user's typed value. The UI combines two different records.

Stable keys do not prevent all list bugs, but they preserve the intended identity mapping. They also let React move an existing keyed subtree rather than throwing it away when only its position changes.

sections.title: What happens after a reorder
sections.content:
| Key choice | Match after reorder | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `contact.id` | Same contact to same component | State follows contact |
| Array index | Same position to new contact | State may follow position |
| `Math.random()` | No previous match | Every row remounts |

sections.title: Keep an ID with the record
Boundary to remember
sections.content: A business value is not automatically a safe key. Names, labels, and timestamps can collide or change. The chosen value must be unique among current siblings and stable for the lifetime of that logical item.

questions.question: How do React keys preserve or reset component state?
questions.title: Keys and component state identity
questions.direct_answer: React associates state with a component's type, position, and key in the render tree. Keeping the same type and key in the same parent preserves that component identity even if keyed siblings reorder. Changing the key gives React a new identity, so the old subtree is removed and a fresh subtree with initial state is created.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner sees key as identity rather than a list-warning attribute.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a changing key to force updates, unintentionally destroying draft state and focus.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both legitimate uses: preserving reordered rows and resetting a form for a new entity.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: State belongs to a component identity in the render tree.
Stable keys keep list state attached to the correct item.
Changing a key intentionally creates a fresh component instance.
A new key resets all state below that keyed boundary.
Do not use changing keys as a routine way to force rendering.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
React state is not stored inside a function variable. React associates it with a component's identity at a position in the rendered tree. Element type and position normally establish that identity, and a key lets the parent name identities among siblings.

In a list, keeping the same key means a row can move while retaining the state for the same logical record. A todo with key `todo-42` remains the `todo-42` component whether it moves from the first position to the fifth. This is why a stable data key prevents editing state from following an index.

Changing the key has a deliberate opposite effect. React treats the next element as a different component, removes the old subtree, and creates a new one with initial state. Every stateful descendant under that boundary resets, and its Effects go through cleanup and setup.

For example, an `EditContact` form may initialize a draft from the selected contact. Rendering `<EditContact key={contact.id} contact={contact} />` gives each contact a separate form identity. Selecting another contact discards the previous draft and starts from the new contact's initial values.

That reset is useful only when the product requirement says the entity changed and old local state should not survive. If the draft must be preserved while switching tabs, changing the key is wrong; state should move to an owner that survives or be stored by contact ID. I therefore use stable keys to preserve identity and a deliberate different key to reset an entire state boundary. I do not add timestamps or random keys to make a component update—state or props should describe a normal update without destroying the instance.

sections.title: A key names a state boundary
sections.content: The component function can be identical while its identity differs. A parent key tells React whether this child continues an earlier stateful lifetime or begins a new one.

sections.title: Reset includes the whole subtree
sections.content:
When a keyed component is replaced, React does not clear only one useState value. It tears down the old component subtree: local state is forgotten, DOM nodes may be replaced, refs detach, and Effect cleanup runs. The new identity mounts from scratch.

This makes a key reset powerful and coarse. It is excellent for changing from one independent form session to another, but too destructive for correcting one field. Ordinary state updates should handle smaller changes.

sections.title: Same type, different identity
sections.content:
`<EditContact key="ada" />` → draft and Effects for Ada
                  key changes
`<EditContact key="grace" />` → fresh draft and Effects for Grace

sections.title: Reset a form when its entity changes
Boundary to remember
sections.content: Keys are scoped to the immediate parent. Giving an inner DOM node a key does not reset state owned by an outer component, and moving a component under a different parent still changes its position and identity even if its key text is the same.

questions.question: Where should a React key be placed, and can a component read it as a prop?
questions.title: Key placement, Fragments, and ordinary props
questions.direct_answer: Place the key on the React element created directly for each item in the surrounding array. An extracted child cannot read `props.key` because React reserves `key` for reconciliation. Pass the same ID separately when the child needs it. For multiple sibling nodes per item, use `<Fragment key={id}>`; the short Fragment syntax cannot take a key.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can apply keys correctly after extracting components or returning multiple nodes.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Placing key on an element inside the child or attempting to read `props.key`.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that the parent performing reconciliation needs the key at its sibling boundary.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Key the element returned directly by the collection's map.
Moving row markup into a component moves the key to that component element.
`key` is reserved and is not available through props.
Pass a separate ID prop when child logic needs the identifier.
Use explicit Fragment syntax when a fragment needs a key.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A key belongs on the React element that is directly created for each item in a collection. The parent owns that sibling array and uses the keys to match its children, so the identity hint must exist at that boundary.

If a map returns an `li` directly, the `li` gets the key. If the row is extracted into a `ContactRow` component, the `ContactRow` element in the map gets the key. Putting a key on an `li` inside `ContactRow` does not identify the `ContactRow` siblings to their parent.

React reserves `key` for reconciliation and does not include it in the component's props object. If `ContactRow` needs the contact ID for an event, test selector, or label relationship, I pass it separately—for example, `<ContactRow key={contact.id} contactId={contact.id} />`.

For example, one record may need to render a heading and paragraph without an extra wrapper node. The explicit `<Fragment key={section.id}>` form groups those siblings and accepts the key. The short `<>...</>` Fragment syntax cannot receive a key, so it is not sufficient in that map.

Key uniqueness is local to the sibling array. The same ID can be used in another list, and a child can create its own separately keyed list. The key should come from the mapped record rather than from data hidden deeper in the child because the parent needs it before that child renders. The placement rule is therefore structural: identify each direct sibling where the array is built, and pass business identifiers through ordinary props when application code needs them. Key and ID may contain the same value, but they serve different consumers.

sections.title: The reconciler and the component need different inputs
sections.content: React consumes `key` while matching a parent's children. The child consumes ordinary props while rendering. Supplying both with the same record ID is intentional, not redundant, because they cross different interfaces.

sections.title: Extraction changes the direct sibling
sections.content:
Before extraction, the map may return `li` elements, so those are the sibling identities. After extraction, the map returns `ContactRow` elements, and their internal `li` nodes sit one level lower. The key follows the direct element created by the map.

An explicit Fragment is also a React element and can carry identity. It groups several output nodes without adding a DOM wrapper, making it appropriate when a record naturally produces adjacent cells, headings, or description rows.

sections.title: The correct keyed boundary
sections.content:
ContactList
├─ ContactRow key=a  ← parent matches here
│  └─ li              ← implementation detail
└─ ContactRow key=b
   └─ li

sections.title: Key an explicit Fragment for each record
Boundary to remember
sections.content: Do not move a key into a reusable child just so callers can omit it. The child does not know whether it is being rendered in a collection or which sibling identity the parent intends. Keys remain a responsibility of the code constructing the collection.
